name: Sorting and Searching Complexity
intent: Know what sorting and searching really cost: the n log n floor for comparison sorts, why the worst case of an algorithm matters, when sorting pays for itself, and when a heap or a counting sort beats sorting everything.
scenario: A service sorts 1,000 records and then answers lookups against them. In testing, with random data, a hand-written quicksort looks fast. In production the input arrives already sorted and the same code needs 499,500 comparisons instead of about 12,000. Meanwhile a report sorts a whole table to show the top 10, and a lookup helper sorts its list on every call.
problem: Sorting and searching are everywhere, and their costs are easy to misjudge. An algorithm that is fast on typical data can be quadratic on a pattern nobody tested. Sorting can be the right call or pure waste depending on how often you search afterwards. Library sorts hide choices (stable or not, comparison-based or not), and small mistakes in a binary search or a comparator turn into wrong answers or endless loops.

howItWorks.title: Comparison sorts have a floor
howItWorks.text: A sort that learns about the order only by comparing two items needs at least about log2(n!) comparisons in the worst case, which is about n log2 n: 8,728 comparisons for merge sort on 1,000 random items, and a million items need only about 2,000 times the comparisons of a thousand items, not a million times. Insertion sort needs 256,407 on the same list because it can move an item one place per comparison. Big O is about growth, and n log n against n squared is the difference between a minute and a week at large n.

howItWorks.title: The worst case is a property of the input pattern
howItWorks.text: Quicksort with the first element as pivot is fast on random data (12,469 comparisons for 1,000 items) but each partition peels off a single item when the input is already sorted, so it needs 499,500, which is n(n-1)/2. Merge sort splits in the middle whatever the data looks like, so it needs about n log n on every pattern. Real libraries typically use hybrids (a version of introsort or Timsort) that choose pivots carefully, switch strategy when a recursion goes bad, and use insertion sort for tiny ranges.

howItWorks.title: Search by halving needs sorted data
howItWorks.text: Binary search looks at the middle item and discards half of the rest, so it needs about log2 n comparisons: 20 for a million items, against up to 1,000,000 for a linear scan. But it only works on sorted data, so the sort is a cost you pay once. With 1,000 items, sorting costs 8,728 comparisons, a linear search averages about 500 and a binary search about 10, so sorting first wins from about 18 searches. Below that, scanning is cheaper.

howItWorks.title: Stability and keys decide what a sort can do
howItWorks.text: A stable sort keeps equal items in their original order, which is what lets you sort by one field and then by another. Merge sort and insertion sort are stable; a plain quicksort is not. When keys are small integers, counting or radix sort avoid comparisons altogether, but counting sort costs n plus the size of the key range: 67,532 steps for 1,000 keys up to 100,000, and only 2,010 for 1,000 keys with 10 distinct values.

howItWorks.title: Sort less than everything
howItWorks.text: If you need only the k largest of n items, keep a min-heap of size k and compare each new item with its smallest: about n log k comparisons instead of n log n (1,171 against 8,728 for the top 10 of 1,000 random items). If you need only the minimum or maximum, one scan of n - 1 comparisons beats any sort. Choosing the right amount of ordering is usually a bigger win than choosing a faster sort.

pros: Sorted data makes searching cost about log n and makes merging, grouping and de-duplicating cheap
Library sorts are tuned hybrids that are fast in practice on most inputs
A heap gives top-k in n log k without sorting everything
Non-comparison sorts can beat n log n when keys are small integers
cons: Sorting costs n log n up front, so it only pays off if the order is used many times
Some fast-on-average sorts have a quadratic worst case on patterns such as sorted input
Sorted data must be kept sorted: every insert into a sorted array costs O(n) moves
Stability, comparator mistakes and special values such as NaN make results subtly wrong
whenToUse: Many searches, range queries or merges over the same data, so one sort is amortised
Data that arrives sorted or nearly sorted, where a good hybrid is close to linear
Top-k needs, where a heap or a selection algorithm replaces a full sort
whenNotToUse: A handful of lookups: a linear scan is cheaper than sorting first
Finding only the minimum or maximum: one pass is enough
A comparison sort for large arrays of small integer keys, where counting or radix sort is better
A hand-written sort in production: use the library's, and spend the effort on the comparator and the keys
pitfalls: Sorting inside a loop: 100 lookups that each re-sort 1,000 items cost 872,800 comparisons against 8,728 for sorting once
Sorting to find the minimum or maximum: sorting 1,000 items costs 8,728 comparisons where a scan costs 999
Trusting a quicksort that was only tested on random data: with a naive pivot, sorted input needs n(n-1)/2 comparisons
Binary search off-by-one errors: using lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 can loop forever once the range is two items wide; decide whether the range is inclusive or half-open and keep it
Comparing floating-point values with NaN: NaN is neither smaller nor larger than anything, so an inconsistent comparator can leave the list unsorted or confuse the algorithm

Sorting by a computed key that is recomputed in every comparison: 1,000 items need about 17,456 key computations that way, against 1,000 if the keys are computed once first (decorate, sort, undecorate)

Assuming a sort is stable when the library does not promise it: check the documentation (JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort is stable since ES2019 and Python's sort is stable, but C++ std::sort and .NET Array.Sort are typically not)

quiz.question: A quicksort that always takes the first item as its pivot sorts 1,000 items that are already in order. About how many comparisons does it make?
options: About 10,000, since it still halves the list on every pass.
About 1,000, because sorted data needs only one pass to confirm.
About 5,000, because the pivot lands in the middle half the time.
About 500,000, since each pass removes only the pivot from the range.
quiz.explanation: With the smallest item as pivot every partition splits 0 and n-1, so the work is 999 + 998 + ... + 1 = 499,500 comparisons, quadratic growth. On random data the same code needs about 12,000. Library sorts avoid this with better pivots or a fallback.

quiz.question: Sorting 1,000 items costs about 8,700 comparisons. A linear search averages about 500 comparisons and a binary search about 10. When is sorting first cheaper?
options: After about 18 searches, once the saved comparisons add up to the sort's cost.
From the very first search, because binary search is always faster than a scan.
Only after about 8,700 searches, one for every comparison the sort made.
Never, since a sort of n items always costs more than n scans.
quiz.explanation: Each search saves about 490 comparisons, so 8,700 / 490 is about 18 searches. Before that the one-off sort costs more than it saves. Binary search is fast per query but needs the sorted order, which has a price.

quiz.question: A report needs the 10 largest of 10 million values. Which approach does the least work?
options: Sort all 10 million values and take the last 10.
Keep a heap of 10 and compare each value with its smallest.
Run a binary search for each of the 10 largest values.
Use counting sort because it never compares any values.
quiz.explanation: A min-heap of size 10 costs about one comparison per value, plus a few for the values that enter the heap: n log k instead of n log n. Binary search needs sorted data, and counting sort costs the size of the key range, which can be huge.
